blocks.text: 2. Postscript to the Corrected Edition of the Diamond Sutra

inline.s: The Diamond Cutter of Perfect Wisdom. Since the Tang dynasty, its upholding and practice have spread throughout the world. As those who copied and printed it grew many, the errors and corruptions in the text multiplied day by day. Shengguan received this sutra when a youth of twenty; at first he merely followed the current text in recitation, without understanding its meaning or even discerning whether the readings differed. In the closing years of the Guangxu reign of the fallen Qing, the Jinling engraving of Master Zhi's commentary was completed. Savoring its commentary, I found much that did not accord with the wording of the present edition, and so a doubt began to stir. I thereupon widely searched the old prints, and further found the commentaries of Zhao and Hui in the Japanese supplement to the canon, and my doubt deepened all the more. When at last I saw the Tang copy of the sutra in the fine hand of Liu Chengxuan, it agreed with the old commentaries; only then did I realize how numerous were the spurious errors of the present edition. Subsequently, receiving an appointment, I collated the Tang manuscripts from the Dunhuang cave in the collection of the Beiping Library; among them the Diamond Sutra was the most numerous, and they largely agreed with Liu's copy. I was deeply moved that the propagation of error and the perpetuation of mistakes had extended so far. Now, having fortunately obtained the genuine trace of the ancients and their old commentaries, the confusion of more than a thousand years stands thereby proven. Why not engrave them and spread them in the world to set it right? Yet long has the false been accepted as the true; like the man of Jing who presented a rough stone, the true connoisseurs are few. I should wait for the opportune moment and not act in haste. This was about the eighth or ninth year of the Republic. In the year gengwu, a certain layman Guo of Chaoyang made a fine engraving of this sutra, saying that it followed Liu's copy. When the book appeared, there were plenty who denounced him for arbitrarily altering the text; yet in fact his engraving did not fully follow Liu's copy. How deep the habit of taking the false for the true! Even so, the excellences of the old edition cannot be concealed. Let me cite a single instance or two. The old edition in the first section reads: ying yun he zhu, "how should it be made to abide?"; the second section reads: yun he ying zhu, "how should it abide?" A single character shifting position, and the meaning is wholly different. Since the false text became the uniform pattern, some have mistakenly taken the passage for a repetition. The sentence "is named," sometimes present and sometimes absent, each case harbors its precise meaning. Since the false text made it appear everywhere, many explained it by the Three Truths. They do not know that prajna correctly sets forth the Two Truths: in the Two Truths, negation and illumination are simultaneous, and that is the Middle. Is there a Middle apart from the Two Truths? The Tiantai school explains all dharmas by the Three Truths; yet Master Zhiyi's commentary on this very sutra throughout reveals the dharmas of dependent origination to be nothing but provisional designations, hence "then it is not." Attaining this "then it is not," one accords with the real and true. As to "is named," he takes it only as a provisional designation—this is truly the skillfully expounded Three Truths. If one must cling to the words of the Three Truths and match "is named" to the Middle, as in "is named adorned," that is acceptable; but "is named the view of self, the view of others, the view of beings, the view of a life span"—how is that to be cleared up? In the autumn of the year renshen, answering the long-standing promise of my friends, I lectured on this sutra, wholly according to the Tang manuscript, while fusing the import of the treatises and the old commentaries. The assembly rejoiced and leapt, and asked that the corrected edition be printed and spread, so that all might know that there is indeed a basis for it, and that what is correct and what is false be made plainly clear to the world. I have appended collation notes after the sutra, citing the various editions and the exegeses of the several schools, sparing no detail, that they may serve for re-checking; and I have set down its origin here. The arising of any undertaking is never unrelated to its season—how much more the profound perfection of wisdom! Depending on the words, one arouses contemplation and awakens to the reality-mark; the affinity of words is by no means a small matter. Someone said: the Chan school is itself the perfection of wisdom, yet it does not establish words—why is that? I replied: you are mistaken. The Surangama Sutra says: "To establish a knowing upon the sight of knowing—this is the root of ignorance. Knowing and seeing, with nothing to see—this is nirvana, the undefiled, true and pure." This is the purport of not establishing. How could it annihilate the marks of words! Moreover, are the recorded sayings of the several schools not words? The proverb says: "To interpret the meaning by relying on the words wrongs the Buddhas of the three times; to depart from the sutra by a single word is like the speech of a devil." How much the more, when the difference of a single character makes a great divergence—how can this be slighted! In the spring of the year guiyou, Shengguan respectfully wrote this postscript.
Republic of China, thirty-third year, fourth month, in the cycle jiashen
Respectfully published by the Puhui Great Canon Publishing Association

blocks.text: 3. A Biography of the Layman Jiang Weinong

inline.s: The layman's surname was Jiang, his given name Zhongye (literally "loyal to the cause"), his style Weinong (literally "the flavor of the farm"). His Dharma name was Miaoxu. In his later years he changed his name to Du, with the sobriquet Dingweng (the Old Man of Stillness). In his books he sometimes signed himself Huanzhu (Dwelling in Illusion), sometimes Shengguan (The Contemplative Viewer), choosing the style as the occasion moved him, without any fixed rule. His ancestors had lived in Lingge village in the southern countryside of Jiangning in Jiangsu; because his grandfather, Master Yuefeng, took up office in Hubei, the family settled there. From childhood the layman followed Master Yuefeng in reciting the Diamond Sutra, and throughout his life he never once let it lapse. His father, Master Renwu, was an upright official of the former Qing, known for good governance. The layman passed the provincial examination in the renin year of Guangxu and soon after was appointed to a prefect of Shaanxi; yet, devoted to nourishing his parents and pleasing them, he had no liking for official advancement. Master Renwu served as an official for several decades, through Jiangxi to Sichuan; the layman accompanied him throughout, aiding in his work, and no matter great or small, he handled it personally. In mid-life the layman lost his wife, and, awakening to the impermanence of human life, he gave himself wholeheartedly to the study of the Buddha. Although, at his parents' command, he remarried, yet to be in the world while renouncing the world—this resolve had long since been settled. In the autumn of xinhai, Master Renwu retired on account of age. The layman, serving his parents, returned from Sichuan to Hubei; and then came the revolutionary army, and the family fortune was swept away. Fleeing eastward, he lodged first in Wulin and later in Shanghai. Though homeless and downcast, tasting every hardship, he nurtured his parents and delighted in the Way, bearing it all with equanimity. Master Renwu, steadfast and of lofty integrity, strictly charged the layman never to enter the path of office again; the layman received this teaching with reverence and dared not forget. In the year dingsi Master Renwu passed away. In the midst of his grief, the layman took the opportunity to persuade his mother, the Lady Guo, to keep a long vegetarian rule and recite the Buddha's name. In the spring of wuwu he proffered respect to the great Chan master Weijun and took him as his teacher, receiving the bodhisattva precepts. He exerted himself in investigation and attained a good measure of insight. At that time the drought in the five northern provinces was severe; the layman, entrusted by Jian Zhaonan, carried funds northward, and through the Buddhist Relief Association distributed a hundred thousand, saving very many lives. I first became acquainted with the layman in Shanghai around the xinren years. Later I met him again in Beijing. In the summer of that year, fellow practitioners Xu Wenwei, Mei Guangxi, and others invited Master Dixian of Guanzong Monastery north to lecture on the Sutra of Complete Enlightenment. He compiled lecture notes himself and distributed them to the assembly; but the master spoke from his nature, and outside the notes he unfolded much else. I therefore asked the layman and Huang Shiheng each to record what they heard, taking notes daily, with the layman bringing the whole into a final form. When it was done it was presented to Master Dixian, who approved it and named it the Record of Personally Heard [Teachings on] Complete Enlightenment. At that time the Metropolitan Library had collected more than eight thousand manuscripts from the Dunhuang cave, many of them rare secret texts needing expert collation; so I proposed to the Ministry of Education that the layman be appointed to the task of collation. From wuwu to jiwei, over two years, the layman, amid the fragmentary and disordered scrolls, assembled the Mahayana Shaliputra Sutra Attended Hearing Commentary in one fascicle and the Commentary on the Vimalakirti Sutra, Collected Explanations of Guan Zhong, in two fascicles. In his postscript to the Mahayana Shaliputra Sutra Commentary he said: "I had heard that in the Dunhuang scrolls there were more than ten fascicles of the Shaliputra commentary, lost from the canon. When I came to the library I eagerly took them up, but they were so tangled, spurious, and corrupted as to be almost unreadable. I combed through them, separating and sifting, arranging and linking them; I took the duplicated scrolls and compared them for differences, and where other books could be cited to corroborate the text, I relied on them; where it could not be determined, I left it in doubt. After eight months of labor I transcribed one fascicle, still lacking its beginning and end. Then Fu Zengxiang purchased a fragmentary scroll in which all the missing commentary was contained; and so this secret work of a thousand years was made a complete book." From this one may know the hardship of his gathering, and the inconceivableness of the timing and causes. In his preface to the Commentary on the Vimalakirti Sutra, Guan Zhong Collection, he said: "This commentary I gathered anew amid a myriad fragmentary scrolls; after more than a year of cold and heat I finally collated it into a book, complete from beginning to end, with only a short section missing in the middle, which does not impair the whole. Of the Guan Zhong commentary on the Vimalakirti Sutra, the only one that can still be heard of today is the commentary of Zhao; yet compared with this book, the latter is often more detailed, and I began to see that Zhao's is no longer the original. Moreover, the works of the Shramana School are all fully preserved in this book; and further I have provided a structural analysis, extracting and distinguishing the sections, reaching where they did not reach, and saying what they did not say. It is like gathering the supreme, wondrous flavor and blending and harmonizing it—extracting the essence and employing the great, and the more one tastes it the more delicious it becomes. So likewise, in a single volume myriad subtle meanings are gathered. If one can still the machine of the mind and face it in stillness, taking the different to attain the universal, contemplating the mind to accord with the substance—how then could the import of the sutra remain unclear and the spirit of wisdom unawakened?" This shows how precious the commentary was. In the year gengshen he returned to Shanghai. When his mother, the Lady Guo, fell ill, the layman recited the Great Compassion Mantra over her and had the family devoutly recite the Buddha's name to aid her. At death the Lady Guo sat up, faced the west, pressed her palms together, and passed away reciting the Buddha's name. From then on the layman's faith grew all the firmer. He had long regretted the habitual tendencies of many lives, and thought to rely on the power of the esoteric mantras to dissolve them. He went again to Beijing, where he happened upon the Japanese master Juesui, who devoted himself to the practice of offering to the Great Joyous Saint. The layman gathered a few like-minded colleagues and asked him to set up an altar and transmit it. On the day of its completion, the layman suddenly felt the appearance of a massive body reaching to the boundless above. Juesui said to him: "In this practice you alone have obtained the greatest merit." Soon after, Juesui led the layman to Mount Koya in Japan for the study of Eastern Esoterism, but hindered by other matters he could not apply himself in seclusion. He soon returned home, and with the brothers Jian Zhaonan and Yujie he organized the Gongde Grove Buddhist Sutra Distribution Centre on the shore of Shanghai. He gathered the plate editions of the northern and southern sutra-engraving offices and of the famous mountains, circulating them throughout the country for the wide propagation of the Dharma and the benefit of living beings. The layman once said that Master Huisi of Nanyue's Mahayana Calm-and-Insight was a rare and precious gem among the native Chinese writings, and that Master Zhiyi's Great Calm-and-Insight came forth from it; that if a student does not first grasp the meaning of Nanyue, then in practicing the Great Calm-and-Insight he will hardly gain the essentials. Yet the mind-dharma of Nanyue had long been buried overseas; though it was transmitted to China in the Song, few paid it heed, which I deeply regret. In the summer of xinyou, the layman Nanyuan of Shanghai initiated a lecture assembly; the layman thereupon proposed inviting Master Dixian to lecture on Mahayana Calm-and-Insight. The layman took notes daily, and at the deep, subtle, and recondite places he used roundabout similes to elucidate them. He sought the correction of Master Dixian, going back and forth repeatedly; only in the year guihai did he finish the draft, naming it the Recorded Exposition. Master Dixian, out of modesty, said that seven or eight tenths of this book were the layman's composition, and would not take the authorship; the layman in turn said that Master Dixian had set the whole in motion, and insisted on attributing the authorship to him, the two deferring to each other. Also, fearing that the proper names and classical phrases in the book would be hard to grasp, he revised it again and again. Eight years passed before the work of twenty fascicles was completed and printed. Master Dixian, recognizing the layman's sincerity, consented to put his own name to it; yet in a letter to the layman he said: "The record is not only smooth in wording and meaning; in its crucial points and fathomless purport it is transparent and clear. All this is the outpouring of the old Vimalakirti's exquisitely subtle insight." In the summer of yichou the venerable Bai Puren came south and presided over the Golden Light Dharma Assembly. The colleagues of Shanghai unanimously recommended the layman to assist the venerable in propagating it; thus from Shanghai to Hangzhou to Hunan to Hubei to Xun to Ning, traveling several thousand li, he took charge of the assembly affairs himself, and all was kept in perfect order. Through this opportunity he was able to study Tibetan Esoterism. In the autumn of jisi, answering the invitation of the faithful of Fujian, he went to Fuzhou to expound the Buddha's Dharma, returning only after three months. In the autumn of gengwu he lectured in Shanghai on the Recorded Exposition of Mahayana Calm-and-Insight, finishing only after more than a year. The Mind-Repose Lotus Society was founded and he was elected its head; from then on he often lectured on the Mahayana scriptures in the society and led the members in reciting the Buddha's name and performing repentance. Knowing that the layman had a singular insight into the Diamond Sutra, in the summer of jiaxu I asked him to expound its general meaning to me. Soon the colleagues of the society demanded that it be made public, and so he lectured formally. I took notes each time, and when I had finished I presented them to him for revision; thereafter he wrote the lecture notes himself and gave them to me to copy. When the assembly was complete, the accumulated drafts amounted to four thick volumes. The layman thought them still needing polish, and that what was lacking in the first section must be supplied, before they could become a book. Because he was a layman and many came to seek the Way from him, he could not devote himself wholly to writing; so the colleagues planned a separate quiet chamber and made offerings to him there, cutting off all else, hoping that within a year he might complete the Diamond Sutra lectures. But the layman, each year, when the season of the yellow plum came, invariably fell ill, and the illness lasted several months. Moved also by compassion for the multitudes who had died in the disasters of north and south, he instituted the Great Compassion Repentance and devotedly assisted the departed to transcend; owing to these delays the lectures were never finally completed, though he had already got six or seven tenths of the whole book. His explanations of the Diamond Sutra often set forth what the ancient teachers had not revealed. For example, when the Buddha spoke other sutras he always emitted a great light and moved the earth in six ways, manifesting all manner of auspicious signs; but for the Diamond Cutter of Perfect Wisdom, a sutra of such depth, the text merely says that at mealtime the World-Honored One donned his robe and took his bowl and entered the great city of Shravasti to beg for food. The layman explained it thus: "The greatest purport of this sutra is to unfold the principle of not dwelling in marks. Hence the opening records the World-Honored One's actions, [which were] identical with those of an ordinary bhiksu—that is, having become a Buddha, he yet does not dwell in the marks of a Buddha; and his disciples too regarded it as ordinary. Only Subhuti perceived his intent, and so praised it as rare and wonderful. Otherwise, holding a bowl and begging for food—what is there to cause such amazement?" In the common edition of the Diamond Sutra, the two rounds of questions both read yun he ying zhu, "how should one abide?" The layman, relying on the old commentaries and the Dunhuang manuscripts, determined that the first section reads ying yun he zhu and the second yun he ying zhu, and that the meaning of the two questions is by no means the same. He explained: "The first section's ying yun he zhu asks how the bodhi-mind should be established in abiding, so that it does not scatter wildly—this is said for one who has just been aroused to great mind and is beginning to practice. The second section's yun he ying zhu asks: since one ought to arouse the mind apart from all marks, how is it that the bodhi-mind alone should abide? If it does not abide in this dharma, then what is called arousing the mind? If one should not abide and should subdue, is that not failing to arouse the mind? Then how is the mind subdued? This is said for one who has already aroused great mind and is practicing." His unfolding of the sublime meaning of the Diamond Sutra was penetrating in just this way; these are but one or two instances I have briefly cited. In the early summer of the year wuyin, with the weather damp and gloomy, the layman was ill as usual, his digestion unwell. I went to see him every two or three days, and found him bedridden and unable to rise, worse than in previous years, and I was deeply concerned. The layman said: "Once the yellow plum season is past, my illness will vanish suddenly." His disciples, in a separate room's Buddha hall, recited the Buddha's name for him, the name sounding without interruption all day long. The layman lay at ease silently reciting, his mind perfectly clear. By mid-fifth month of the lunar calendar his illness worsened, but his clarity of mind at greater. His fellow practitioner Zhu Guangqi wrote in large red characters urging him to single-mindedly seek rebirth and not cling to the world. The layman examined it several times, pressed his palms together to thank Zhu, and spoke words of joy and praise. After Zhu left, he said to those about him: "I have diligently practiced all my life—could I be still unable to settle this one barrier? Master Zhu is overly anxious, I fear." On the night of the eighteenth he said of himself: "A golden light shines everywhere; the Buddha comes to lead me." He summoned his fellow practitioners, and Cai Jiping, delayed by affairs, arrived only at midnight. The layman still instructed him: "In practice, the most important thing is the vows of conduct of Samantabhadra." Then he pressed his palms together and spoke no more, and amid the sound of the Buddha's name from his fellow practitioners and family, he passed away in peace. He was sixty-seven. My friendship with the layman lasted more than twenty years. At first I knew only that he had ranged over the various schools and taken refuge in the Pure Land; in recent years our mutual friendship grew deeper and our investigation of the Dharma deeper still, and only then did I learn that the layman throughout his life drew his strength from prajna, that giving himself to profound investigation he had long attained insight, and that, breaking open in full enlightenment, his single mind was ever within concentration, and that at night he had no dreams—and this for more than five years. Hence he often said of himself: "My teaching rests on prajna; my practice lies in Amitabha." When he spoke the Dharma, he spoke from his nature, reaching all roundabout and direct, at ease without obstruction. Whenever I happened to doubt some point in the scriptures or in the practice of cultivation and consulted him, his answers were always a step above those of others. And the strictness of his precepts and the secrecy of his advancing practice made him a model for a whole generation. Truly the layman was a mighty elephant of the gateway of the Buddha!
